table.header: 2.1. Participants

table.text: We recruited 83 participants (50 female and 33 male; aged 17-65, mean age1 = 21.33 ± 6.12 years) through the university's research participation platform SONA and local advertisements.

table.header: 2.1. Participants

table.text: The remaining 74 participants were assigned to one of two groups: the compound landmark learning group ("CLM"; N = 36; 19 female and 17 male) or the single landmark learning group ("SLM"; N = 38; 23 female and 15 male).
table.header: 2.1. Participants

table.text: Participants were seated comfortably in a chair facing a 24" computer monitor.
table.header: 2.2. Apparatuses

table.text: On test trials, the target was removed from the virtual environment, and the participants were asked to recall and navigate to the location where the target had been previously located using one or both landmarks as reference cue(s) (depending on the type of test trial).
table.header: 2.3. Materials and design

table.text: Participants were tested individually 2 .
table.header: 2.4. Procedure

table.text: Participants were instructed to remember the target position and were informed that they could take as much time as they needed.
table.header: 2.4. Procedure

table.text: Participants were informed that the test trials could present one or both landmarks, but they were not informed that the landmarks could be shifted.
table.header: 2.4. Procedure

table.text: On each test trial, with one or both landmarks shown, participants were first asked to imagine where the target was for 2 seconds during which navigation was not allowed.
table.header: 2.4. Procedure

table.text: Then, participants were instructed to go to the original target's position and press a button on the controller to record their response.
table.header: 2.4. Procedure

table.text: Participants were instructed to be as accurate as possible, and they were allowed to make only one response in each trial.
table.header: 2.4. Procedure

table.text: At the beginning of each trial, participants were repositioned such that they were facing the midpoint of the x-axis between the two landmark positions.
table.header: 2.4. Procedure

table.text: Participants were instructed not to use the starting distance as a cue to remember the target's position, as it would not be reliable.
table.header: 2.4. Procedure

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> We recruited 83 participants (50 female and 33 male; aged 17-65, mean age1 = 21.33 ± 6.12 years) through the university's research participation platform SONA and local advertisements.

> Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.

> Two additional participants were withdrawn due to technical issues with the experimental program or the EEG recording system.

> The remaining 74 participants were assigned to one of two groups: the compound landmark learning group ("CLM"; N = 36; 19 female and 17 male) or the single landmark learning group ("SLM"; N = 38; 23 female and 15 male).

> Participants were seated comfortably in a chair facing a 24" computer monitor.

> On test trials, the target was removed from the virtual environment, and the participants were asked to recall and navigate to the location where the target had been previously located using one or both landmarks as reference cue(s) (depending on the type of test trial).

> Participants were tested individually 2 .

> Participants were instructed to remember the target position and were informed that they could take as much time as they needed.

> Participants were informed that the test trials could present one or both landmarks, but they were not informed that the landmarks could be shifted.

> On each test trial, with one or both landmarks shown, participants were first asked to imagine where the target was for 2 seconds during which navigation was not allowed.

> Then, participants were instructed to go to the original target's position and press a button on the controller to record their response.

> Participants were instructed to be as accurate as possible, and they were allowed to make only one response in each trial.

> At the beginning of each trial, participants were repositioned such that they were facing the midpoint of the x-axis between the two landmark positions.

> Participants were instructed not to use the starting distance as a cue to remember the target's position, as it would not be reliable.

> Participants were grouped into one of the seven categories based on the outcome of this comparison: combination model clearly best, competition model clearly best, strategy selection model clearly best, combination and competition models both plausible (strategy selection model ruled out), combination and strategy selection models both plausible (competition model ruled out), competition and strategy selection models both plausible (combination model ruled out), and not clear (all three models plausible; ΔAIC ≤ 2 for all).

> Second, participants in the current study learned the target's position only once for each landmark and no feedback was provided during test trials, whereas in Du et al. (2017), participants completed dozens of training trials for the same cue-target representations and received feedback during some single cue test trials.

> It should be noted that we did not directly test whether participants were aware of cue conflicts in the shift test.

Ethics approval statement:

> All procedures were performed in compliance with relevant laws and institutional guidelines; this study was approved by the Western University Non-Medical Research Ethics Board (NMREB #124233).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: We recruited 83 participants (50 female and 33 male; aged 17-65, mean age1 = 21.33 ± 6.12 years) through the university's research participation platform SONA and local advertisements.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
Two additional participants were withdrawn due to technical issues with the experimental program or the EEG recording system.

The remaining 74 participants were assigned to one of two groups: the compound landmark learning group ("CLM"; N = 36; 19 female and 17 male) or the single landmark learning group ("SLM"; N = 38; 23 female and 15 male).
Participants were seated comfortably in a chair facing a 24" computer monitor.

On test trials, the target was removed from the virtual environment, and the participants were asked to recall and navigate to the location where the target had been previously located using one or both landmarks as reference cue(s) (depending on the type of test trial).
Participants were instructed to remember the target position and were informed that they could take as much time as they needed.
Participants were informed that the test trials could present one or both landmarks, but they were not informed that the landmarks could be shifted.
On each test trial, with one or both landmarks shown, participants were first asked to imagine where the target was for 2 seconds during which navigation was not allowed.
Then, participants were instructed to go to the original target's position and press a button on the controller to record their response.
Participants were instructed to be as accurate as possible, and they were allowed to make only one response in each trial.
At the beginning of each trial, participants were repositioned such that they were facing the midpoint of the x-axis between the two landmark positions.

Second, participants in the current study learned the target's position only once for each landmark and no feedback was provided during test trials, whereas in Du et al. (2017), participants completed dozens of training trials for the same cue-target representations and received feedback during some single cue test trials.
It should be noted that we did not directly test whether participants were aware of cue conflicts in the shift test.

text.text: Cue combination and competition in navigation have been observed among various spatial cues, yet it remains unclear whether the decision to combine cues is driven by the uncertainties of individual cues or by strategy-level competition.
To address this, we examined whether compound or single cue learning experience can influence the selection of cue combination or competition.

Participants learned target locations in a virtual environment with two landmarks and were assigned to either the compound learning group (who encoded the target with both landmarks) or the single learning group (who learned from one landmark at a time).
In the testing phase, participants recalled the target location under single-cue, compound, and landmark-shift (conflict) conditions.
In compound tests, both groups showed lower variances than in single-cue tests, indicating optimal cue combination based on single-cue uncertainties.
In shift tests, however, despite optimal cue weights, no variance reduction was observed, and the variances were inconsistent with both cue combination and competition models.

Using a maximum likelihood estimation approach, we estimated the probability of using the combination strategy and found that learning experience systematically modulated this probability: The majority of the compound learning group showed high probabilities of combination, whereas the single learning group showed large individual differences.

AIC model comparisons indicate that our strategy selection model, which incorporates the estimated probability of combination, provided a better fit to the observed data than pure combination or competition models, especially in shift tests.
These results support the strategy-mediated account, suggesting a potential decision-making process in cue combination.
Navigating one's environment is an essential ability for survival.
Successful navigation involves accurate encoding and retrieval of information from multiple sources.

For example, a navigator in a forest may use multiple spatial cues (a creek, a tall oak tree, an oddly shaped rock, etc.) to find their way back to the cave they previously used as shelter on a cold night.
By combining these cues, the uncertainty related to any single cue can be reduced, and the precision of the navigator's estimate about the target location can be improved (Newman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: By combining these cues, the uncertainty related to any single cue can be reduced, and the precision of the navigator's estimate about the target location can be improved <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Newman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Research studies have demonstrated that navigators will make use of multiple spatial cues (for reviews, see Cheng et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2023) including multiple landmarks (Du et al., 2017; Newman & McNamara, 2022), boundaries and landmarks (Doeller & Burgess, 2008), and path integration and landmarks (Chen & McNamara, 2017; Nardini et al., 2008; Sjolund et al., 2018; L. Zhang et al., 2020; Zhao & Warren, 2015).

Zhang et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Zhao & Warren, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, whether these cues are combined to create a unitary spatial representation of a target's location or maintained as independent relationships between the target and each of the available spatial cues remains unclear.

Furthermore, if independent cue-target representations are maintained, the question of whether a navigator makes behavioral decisions based on a single cue or combines across cues during retrieval is also poorly understood.

Whether spatial relationships are encoded within a unitary representation or combined during retrieval, cue combination could be expected to reduce uncertainty, as the use of multiple cues could lead to a more precise representation of the target location than that provided by even the best individual cue (Cheng et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Whether spatial relationships are encoded within a unitary representation or combined during retrieval, cue combination could be expected to reduce uncertainty, as the use of multiple cues could lead to a more precise representation of the target location than that provided by even the best individual cue <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cheng et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Newman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A common paradigm for examining cue combination is to test participants' memories regarding a target location with both individual cues and compound cue conditions.
Evidence of cue combination in such paradigms is the response variability (often the variance) in the compound cue condition is reduced comparing to the individual cue conditions.

A combined estimate of the target's location would be considered optimal when cues are combined according to their relative reliabilities (e.g., more reliable cues should show lower uncertainties and be given greater weighting), such that variance is reduced to a minimum (Cheng et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A combined estimate of the target's location would be considered optimal when cues are combined according to their relative reliabilities (e.g., more reliable cues should show lower uncertainties and be given greater weighting), such that variance is reduced to a minimum <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cheng et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Newman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, cue weightings have been shown to be related to the relative uncertainty of competing sensory inputs (Cheng et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Indeed, cue weightings have been shown to be related to the relative uncertainty of competing sensory inputs <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cheng et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Newman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: If the relationships between individual spatial cues and target locations are encoded with reasonable accuracy, and information from cues is weighted according to reliability, cue combination could be expected to result in improved navigation.
However, assuming multiple independent cue-target representations are maintained, it is also possible that a navigator might use a single cue-target representation during navigation.
In that case, one cue might be selected as the reference for a given trial, and the target location would be identified based on its spatial relationship to that cue.
Additionally, over the course of many trials, there may be competition among cues, with the outcome of a specific trial reflecting the precision of one of several possible cue-target representations.

Cue competition would thus be expected to result in more uncertainty and less precision in target estimation than one might expect based on the best individual cue (Du et al., 2017; Nardini et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Cue competition would thus be expected to result in more uncertainty and less precision in target estimation than one might expect based on the best individual cue <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Du et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Nardini et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Previous research often employs cue conflict tests to examine cue competition (Newman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Previous research often employs cue conflict tests to examine cue competition <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Newman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In these tests, researchers present compound cues to participants and make some form of modifications to these cues such that they are different from when they are encoded and inconsistent with each other (e.g., intentionally increasing the distance between landmarks).

Under such conditions, response bias towards the most reliable cue is likely to be observed (although responses towards other cues may also occur) and response variability will be increased comparing to the individual cue conditions.

Although the ideas of cue combination and competition have been extensively discussed (e.g., Newman et al., 2023), it remains unclear whether an individual navigator can employ both strategies, and under what circumstances one might be selected over the other.
text.formatted: Although the ideas of cue combination and competition have been extensively discussed (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Newman et al., 2023)</ref>, it remains unclear whether an individual navigator can employ both strategies, and under what circumstances one might be selected over the other.

text.text: As described above, compared to using individual cue-target representations, combining across spatial cues should reduce uncertainty and improve target localization; however, in some circumstances cue combination may not be feasible.

For example, young children appear more likely to use a strategy based on cue competition than combination, showing greater response variability when multiple cues are available than when provided with only a single cue (Nardini et al., 2008).
text.formatted: For example, young children appear more likely to use a strategy based on cue competition than combination, showing greater response variability when multiple cues are available than when provided with only a single cue <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Nardini et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that effective cue combination may require a good deal of experience or rely on cognitive abilities with a protracted developmental timeline.

Moreover, when too many spatial cues are present, adult navigators fail to show evidence of effective cue combination (Scherer et al., 2024), perhaps because computing a unitary representation of the target location becomes too cognitively demanding.
text.formatted: Moreover, when too many spatial cues are present, adult navigators fail to show evidence of effective cue combination <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Scherer et al., 2024)</ref>, perhaps because computing a unitary representation of the target location becomes too cognitively demanding.

text.text: Finally, when the individual cue-target relationships are discordant (i.e., when the target location estimates based on individual spatial cues are non-overlapping), it may be impossible to combine across cues.
Indeed, when facing large conflicts between cues, the effects of cue combination appear weakened or faded (Du et al., 2017; Harootonian et al., 2022; Sjolund et al., 2018; Zhao & Warren, 2015).
text.formatted: Indeed, when facing large conflicts between cues, the effects of cue combination appear weakened or faded <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Du et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Harootonian et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Sjolund et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Zhao & Warren, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Whether a combination or competition strategy is used for navigation is at least partially determined by the amount of information available to the navigator.
For example, when sensory inputs become too complex (e.g., too many landmarks in the environment), adults are less likely to combine across cues than in simpler environments (Scherer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, when sensory inputs become too complex (e.g., too many landmarks in the environment), adults are less likely to combine across cues than in simpler environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Scherer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, both the generation of a combined, weighted representation based on cue reliability and the selection of the most reliable representation among individual competing cues suggest that prior belief and experience may also play a significant role in strategy selection.

A navigator's experience with similar tasks or belief that one spatial cue may be more useful than another is likely to contribute to the baseline weightings of cue reliability that may be used to optimize combination, or affect the likelihood of selecting an individual cue in the case of competition.
Indeed, computational modeling work shows that prior experience is involved in cue combination and influences the cue weighting (McNamara & Chen, 2022; Vishwanath et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Indeed, computational modeling work shows that prior experience is involved in cue combination and influences the cue weighting <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(McNamara & Chen, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Vishwanath et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, strategy selection may depend on the nature of the cues (e.g., cue complexity, cue types, the degree of cue conflict, etc.; bottom-up) and a navigator's experience with those types of cues (top-down).

Depending on the nature of a navigational task, the reliability of the spatial cues involved, and an individual's experience and beliefs, combination and competition strategies may produce different estimates of a target's location.
Thus, the strategy adopted by a navigator can have a significant impact on their performance.

Strategy selection does not appear to be a conscious decision on the part of the navigator; computational work has reinforced that cue combination emerges from dynamic interactions between cues rather than from an explicit strategy selection process (Kessler et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Strategy selection does not appear to be a conscious decision on the part of the navigator; computational work has reinforced that cue combination emerges from dynamic interactions between cues rather than from an explicit strategy selection process <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kessler et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether a single strategy is adopted for a given task, or whether the target representations produced by both strategies are both available to the navigator on any given trial and are, thus, also in competition.

The current study proposes the latter, suggesting that navigators choose between combination-and competitionbased strategies based on their experience (both long-term and recent) and the similarity between the current trial and the way they have been trained to perform a specific navigational task.
Based on previous work (Du et al., 2017; Newman et al., 2022), the current study focused on navigating to a target based on its proximity to multiple visual landmarks.

text.text: Specifically, we presented participants with a desktop virtual reality navigation-and-localization task with two visual landmarks.
Participants first learned a target object's location via virtual navigation in the presence of one or both of these landmarks and were later asked to recall the target's location (Figure 1).

text.text: To examine the potential effect of recent experience on subsequent recall, participants either experienced compound cues (i.e., the presence of two landmarks presented at the same time) or isolated cues (i.e., the same landmarks presented one at a time) during learning trials.

If strategy selection is determined solely by exposure to the cues in the environment, the two groups would be expected to show similar probabilities of selecting a cue combination/competition strategy, since the visual information provided in training was equivalent across learning conditions.

However, if recent experience of encoding compound or isolated cues also affects strategy selection, the compound learning group would be expected to show an increased probability of selecting the combination strategy compared to the group who learned the cue-target representations independently (e.g., Newman et al., 2023).

text.text: Performance was measured on test trials in which the spatial cues were presented in isolation, and in which the cues were presented simultaneously in the positions they occupied during learning ("compound condition") and shifted away from those positions ("shift condition").
Response variability in the compound and the shift condition trials was compared to single cue trials to determine when navigators showed evidence of cue combination/competition.

Finally, performance on trials showing evidence of cue combination was compared to optimal predicted responses to assess how appropriately navigators were able to weight the available spatial cues when responding (Chen et al., 2017; Du et al., 2017; Sjolund et al., 2018; Newman et al., 2022).

text.text: These specific learning and test conditions will allow us to determine if there is strategy-level competition in navigational decision making and how recent learning experience may influence this competition.

The remaining 74 participants were assigned to one of two groups: the compound landmark learning group ("CLM"; N = 36; 19 female and 17 male) or the single landmark learning group ("SLM"; N = 38; 23 female and 15 male).

On test trials, the target was removed from the virtual environment, and the participants were asked to recall and navigate to the location where the target had been previously located using one or both landmarks as reference cue(s) (depending on the type of test trial).
The task consisted of 24 blocks, where each block included a learning phase with one or two trials and four test trials.

The key difference between the two groups was the learning phase: the CLM group always learned the target's position in a single trial with both landmarks presented simultaneously (i.e., compound cue learning), while the SLM group learned the target's position over two trials with each landmark presented in isolation on each trial (i.e., single cue learning).
For the SLM group, which landmark was learned first was counterbalanced across blocks.

text.text: Spatial navigation is an essential cognitive task that requires the accurate encoding of multiple sources of information from the environment and their interactions, which may involve different strategies across individuals and environments.

The current study asks whether there is competition between these different strategies when a navigator is presented with multiple spatial cues, each of which has a unique relationship to the target location.

Using a virtual navigation and localization task, we observed responses consistent with cue combination when two landmark cues were simultaneously presented at the same positions they occupied on target location learning trials, regardless of whether cue-target representations were learned simultaneously or sequentially.
However, when the landmarks were shifted away from their previously learned positions, a conflict was created between cue-target representations and cue combination was no longer observed.
Additionally, we found that prior learning experience (with compound cues and single cues) affected the likelihood that a given navigator would employ a cue combination strategy.

Among the different strategies (cue combination, cue competition, or strategy selection) that were compared to determine which provided the best fit to the behavioural response data, strategy-selection was the best performing model, especially in the shift test (Table 2).

text.text: Therefore, individual cue-target representations in Du et al. (2017) were enhanced through extensive encoding and resulted in small variances in single cue tests compared to compound test trials which were presented only a handful of times.

text.text: These differences in familiarly across trial types were better controlled in the current study.

Although the empirical weighting ascribed to the near landmark in the shift test was consistent with the optimal weight predicted by the combination model (Figure 4), the observed variability in localization responses was not consistent with what was predicted by the combination model or the competition model for either group of learners (Figure 3).

text.text: This is consistent with previous findings that when faced with conflict, humans are less likely to combine cues (Du et al., 2017; Harootonian et al., 2022; Sjolund et al., 2018; Zhao & Warren, 2015).

text.text: Instead, the variability observed in the shift test was best described by the strategyselection model.
Large conflicts between cues may cause competition between multiple candidate representations (Harootonian et al., 2022).

text.text: According to the recently proposed Bayesian casual inference model (Chen, Chen, et al., 2025), awareness of large cue conflicts indicates uncommon sources of cues and thus the lower cue weighting assigned to the more unstable, noisier cue and increased sensory noises on that cue.

text.text: It should be noted that we did not directly test whether participants were aware of cue conflicts in the shift test.
Even if they were aware of the cue conflicts, it seems they did not reconcile the conflicts and follow the cue combination strategy.

It is worth noting that no individual participant's pattern of results was best fit by a pure cue combination or cue competition model, even when the spatial cues were identical across learning and testing trials (i.e., compound test trials for compound learners;
Figure 5A-D and Figure S5).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5A-D</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">S5</ref>).

text.text: It is worth noting that, while the way in which cue-target representations were learned in the current study (i.e., compound vs. single cue learning) had an effect on subsequent test trial performance, participants also have a great deal of experience with real life spatial navigation, where combining representations from multiple landmarks would be expected to improve performance relative to alternating between single landmarks.
This longer-term learning might be expected to result in a natural preference for cue combination over competition that may have also affected their patterns of behavior in the current study.
For example, if the current task is considered novel relative to their typical navigation experiences, individuals may default to a familiar strategy (cue combination).

Thus, the effect of cue learning in the current experiment was likely either congruent (compound learning group) or incongruent (single learning group) with an individual's longer-term experience; this may have produced group level differences in the extent to which cue combination vs competition-based strategies were employed during test trials.

These group level differences would be expected to be most apparent during shift test trials, where conflicting cue-target representations may have required participants to re-evaluate their strategy rather than simply relying upon the one they used on compound trials.

Indeed, the degree to which navigators appeared to use cue combination in the compound vs. shift tests was not correlated across participants, as the best model fit across tests was not consistent for all participants (Figure S5).

text.text: These results are in line with the idea that conflicts judged to arise from different causes (e.g., the judgment that a particular cue-target representation is unstable due to the shifting of a landmark) evoke a top-down approach to weighting the reliability of competing representations (Chen, Chen, et al., 2025).

text.text: It is possible that the selection between combination and competition-based strategies was reset on each trial, suggesting cognitive flexibility in navigation.
We observed broad individual differences in the likelihood of adopting a cue combination strategy.
While most participants in the compound learning group overwhelmingly favored cue combination, a few participants showed surprisingly low probabilities of employing this strategy.
Similar evidence of individual differences in rotation and straight-line translation navigation tasks has been observed previously (Harootonian et al., 2022; Vishwanath et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Similar evidence of individual differences in rotation and straight-line translation navigation tasks has been observed previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Harootonian et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Vishwanath et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that in addition to the effects of learning, strategy choice may also depend upon an individual's cognitive style, uncertainty tolerance, or preference for fixed vs. heuristic strategies.
Future research is needed to further examine how these aspects might influence strategy choice.
Our strategy selection model proposes that when faced with a navigational task, there is competition between multiple strategies.

The plausibility of this model is supported by the observation that humans can process multiple spatial representations in parallel (Chen, Wei, et al., 2025; Harootonian et al., 2022; Ishikawa & Montello, 2006; H. Zhang et al., 2014).

Zhang et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, our results suggest that despite parallel processing, not all representations may be equally accessible or active at any given moment; rather, the extent to which a given representation is accessed appears to vary as a function of experience (both long-term and task-specific) and the accordance between cue-target representations.
Maintaining multiple representations at the same time allows different cues to be evaluated and used, making it adaptive in an environment with changing conditions.
